method: Headlines from the source feed, read by Claude: summary and four beats in Blue Street's own words from each article's headline and public text; impact = which way the headline pushes each market (dir bullish/bearish/mixed, strength 1 mild, 2 clear, 3 strong). Evidence, not a call.

USD.text: Democrats won both the US Senate and the House in Tuesday's midterm elections, and the dollar fell to a one-month low as US yields dropped. Thursday's stock crash left the dollar flat, as safe-haven buying met lower yields and bets that the next Federal Reserve rise comes later; Friday's jobs report will show whether that view holds.

EUR.text: The euro is near $1.127, close to a one-month high, mostly because the dollar fell after Democrats won the US Congress. At home the news is middling: inflation rose to 4.0% in October as expected, keeping a December European Central Bank rate rise in view, while German factory orders bounced back in September by a little less than forecast.

GBP.text: The Bank of England raised its rate to 4% on Thursday, its first rise since 2023, and now expects UK inflation to climb to about 5% next year because of higher energy costs from the Iran war. Governor Andrew Bailey said another rise could follow unless the Middle East conflict moves toward a settlement, which supports the pound, already near its highest since mid-September on a weaker dollar.

JPY.text: Stocks in Tokyo fell more than 6% early on Friday after Wall Street's worst day in over a year, and US yields slipped, which usually helps the yen; yet it barely moved, near 157.8 per dollar. Bank of Japan minutes show the board wants more rate rises, but dearer oil, which Japan imports almost entirely, keeps weighing on the currency.

CHF.text: Swiss inflation jumped to 1.5% in October on dearer fuel, which makes a December rate cut by the Swiss National Bank harder to justify. Thursday's sharp fall in US stocks and more tanker attacks near Hormuz add to demand for the franc as a safe place to park money.

CAD.text: The Canadian dollar reached a seven-week high this week on a bigger trade surplus and a weaker US dollar, and oil, Canada's main export, bounced back on Thursday. Thursday's federal budget added C$142 billion of measures and keeps deficits above C$50 billion a year, but most of it was known; the slump in US stocks is the bigger drag.

AUD.text: The Australian dollar fell 1% on Thursday, the most of the major currencies, as US stocks had their worst day in over a year on a crash in chip shares. The Reserve Bank of Australia's rise to 4.85% on Tuesday and its warning that inflation is still too high give some support, but for now the global sell-off weighs more.

NZD.text: New Zealand's jobless rate rose to 5.7% in the third quarter, its highest since 2015, which makes further Reserve Bank of New Zealand rate cuts more likely. Slower services growth in China, its biggest customer, adds to the pressure, while a third straight rise in global dairy prices is the main support.

XAU.text: Gold climbed to about $4,135 an ounce on Thursday, its highest since late October, after a 3.5% jump on Wednesday as the dollar and US yields fell on the Democratic sweep of Congress; central banks also kept buying last quarter. Markets still expect a December Federal Reserve rate rise, so Friday's US jobs report decides whether the rebound holds.

OIL.text: Brent crude fell to a two-month low near $93 on Wednesday on bets the new Democratic Congress pushes Washington to end the Iran war, then climbed back to about $98 on Thursday as more tankers were hit near the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has since sent the US a nuclear proposal through Qatar, but says it won't reopen Hormuz until its seven demands are met, so supply risk stays.

items.headline: Japan's Nikkei falls more than 6% and South Korea's Kospi about 7% as the AI-stock sell-off spreads to Asia
items.story_title: AI stocks sell off after the US midterms
items.summary: Tokyo's Nikkei 225 fell more than 6% and Seoul's Kospi about 7% early on Friday, following Wall Street's worst day in over a year. The yen barely moved, near 157.8 per dollar.

beats.was: Democrats won both houses of the US Congress on Tuesday, raising worries about tighter rules on artificial intelligence and slower building of data centres. On Thursday the Nasdaq fell 5.5% and the S&P 500 4.4% as chip shares crashed.
beats.happened: In Friday morning trading the Nikkei dropped about 6.2% and the Kospi about 7.1%, both heavy in chip and tech makers. Australia's ASX 200 fell a milder 0.7%. US 10-year yields eased to about 4.84%.
beats.means: The sell-off has moved from New York to Asia's tech-heavy markets, so worry about global growth is spreading. Falls this big usually pull money toward safer assets and away from growth-linked currencies.
beats.fx: The yen held near 157.8 per dollar rather than jumping, as dearer oil still weighs on Japan; the Korean won and the Australian dollar are the most exposed.

impact.why: Safe-haven pull and lower US yields help, but the yen hardly moved as Tokyo stocks sank.
Asia's stock slump adds to Thursday's hit to the most growth-linked major currency.
Tends to fall with the Australian dollar when risk appetite drops.
Investors tend to park money in the franc during steep stock sell-offs.

items.watch: Whether European and US stocks steady on Friday, and the US jobs report for October at 7:30 AM CT.

items.headline: Canada's budget adds C$142 billion in new measures and keeps deficits above C$50 billion a year
items.story_title: Canada's 2026 budget
items.summary: Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne tabled Canada's 2026 budget on Thursday, with C$142.1 billion of new tax breaks and spending over five years and no plan to balance the books.

beats.was: Prime Minister Mark Carney's government had promised a budget aimed at lifting growth and investment, while the parliamentary budget watchdog warned deficits were getting bigger.
beats.happened: This year's deficit is put at C$62.3 billion, about C$3 billion less than projected in the spring, with deficits above C$50 billion in each of the next four years. The biggest item is a C$36.1 billion tax break for business investment, announced earlier.
beats.means: Much of the plan was already known, so it brings few surprises for markets. More borrowing adds a little pressure on Canadian bond yields over time and gives the Bank of Canada one more reason to watch inflation.
beats.fx: Little direct effect on the Canadian dollar for now; oil prices and the US dollar matter more this week.

impact.why: Large, mostly expected spending: growth support versus more debt.

items.watch: Whether the budget passes a confidence vote in Parliament, and Canada's October jobs report on Friday.

items.headline: Iran's leader says US hostility won't end with the midterms; Trump says the war was needed despite the election loss
items.story_title: Oil and the Iran war after the US midterms
items.summary: Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said the US midterm result won't change Washington's hostility, while President Trump admitted the war largely cost his party the election but said it had to be done.

beats.was: Markets have been betting that Democratic control of the US Congress would push Washington toward ending its war with Iran, which sent oil sharply lower on Wednesday.
beats.happened: Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said US hostility toward Iran will continue whatever the election result. President Donald Trump said the attack on Iran was the main reason Republicans lost, but insisted it was necessary to stop Iran building a nuclear weapon.
beats.means: Neither side is signalling a quick climb-down, which tempers the hope for a fast peace deal that drove oil down.
beats.fx: Tough words from both capitals add a little risk back to oil and to safe havens such as the Swiss franc; actual talks or new attacks would matter far more than words.

impact.why: Hard-line words from both sides cool hopes of a quick settlement.
A lingering war keeps some demand for a safe haven.

items.watch: Whether US-Iran talks resume, and any new strikes or attacks on shipping near Hormuz.

items.headline: Australia's Hauser says inflation is too high on every measure
items.story_title: Reserve Bank of Australia: a fifth rate rise this year?
items.summary: Reserve Bank of Australia Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said inflation is too high however it is measured and warned that public trust in the bank's fight against it is slipping.

beats.was: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its rate to 4.85% on Tuesday, and Governor Michele Bullock then said it was time to pause and see how the rises work.
beats.happened: On Thursday Hauser, the bank's number two, said inflation is too high whichever gauge you use and that public confidence in the bank's ability to bring it down is weakening. He also denied that his remarks in October were meant to push the board toward a rise.
beats.means: His tone is firmer than Bullock's talk of a pause, a reminder that another rise is not ruled out if prices keep running hot. It adds no new data, so it changes little on its own.
beats.fx: Firm words from a senior policymaker give the Australian dollar mild support; it barely moved, holding near 70 US cents.

impact.why: Tough talk on inflation keeps another rate rise possible, but the market barely reacted.

items.watch: Australia's quarterly inflation figures and speeches by Bullock for any shift from the pause message.

items.headline: Bank of Canada's Macklem tells senators another rate rise may be needed but the bank will go carefully
items.story_title: Bank of Canada: a rate rise to fight energy-driven inflation
items.summary: Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem told a Senate committee the bank may have to raise rates again, but with slack in the economy it will decide one meeting at a time.

beats.was: The Bank of Canada raised its rate to 2.5% on October 28, its first rise since July 2023, because the Iran war has kept fuel prices high. Canada's inflation has been about 3%, above the bank's 2% target, since April.
beats.happened: Speaking to the Senate banking committee on Thursday, Macklem said inflation should reach about 3.5% by year-end and stay at or above 3% for much of 2027. He said new US tariffs will likely slow growth late this year and that the economy still has some spare capacity, so the bank will move carefully.
beats.means: This repeats what he told MPs on Tuesday, when he also said federal spending is not really adding to inflation. The door to a December rise stays open, but spare capacity gives the bank room to wait.
beats.fx: Steady words that markets already expected, so little support for the Canadian dollar on their own. Thursday's federal budget and the price of oil, Canada's main export, matter more for now.

impact.why: Keeps a further rate rise possible, but stresses caution and spare capacity.

items.watch: Canada's federal budget, due Thursday afternoon, and the Bank of Canada's next decision on December 9.

items.headline: Wall Street ends its worst day in over a year as chip stocks crash; Australian dollar falls most
items.story_title: AI stocks sell off after the US midterms
items.summary: US stocks closed sharply lower on Thursday, with the Nasdaq down 5.5% and a chip-stock index down about 12%. The Australian dollar fell 1%, the most of the major currencies, while the US dollar barely moved.

beats.was: Democrats won control of both houses of the US Congress on Tuesday, raising worries about tighter rules on artificial intelligence and slower building of data centres. AI and chip shares had driven much of this year's stock gains.
beats.happened: The S&P 500 fell 4.4% and the Dow 3.4%, with every sector lower. The Philadelphia chip index had its second-worst day on record. US 10-year yields slipped to about 4.9%, oil ended 3-4% higher and gold rose about 1%.
beats.means: A sell-off this deep hits currencies tied to global growth and risk appetite first. Traders now see the next Federal Reserve rate rise later, around March 2027, which takes a little support away from the dollar.
beats.fx: The Australian dollar took the biggest hit; the US dollar held steady as falling yields offset its safe-haven pull.

impact.why: The currency most tied to global growth fell 1% as stocks slumped.
Moves with the Australian dollar when risk appetite drops.
Safe-haven demand met lower yields and later Fed rate-rise bets.
Gold rose about 1% as money looked for shelter and yields fell.

items.watch: Friday's US jobs report for October and whether Asian stock markets extend the slide.

items.headline: Iran sends the US a nuclear proposal through Qatar, but only for after its seven conditions are met
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: A senior Iranian official says Iran has passed the US a nuclear proposal through Qatar, and Washington is reviewing it. Iran says it will only discuss it, and only reopen the Strait of Hormuz, once its seven demands are met.

beats.was: The US and Israel have been at war with Iran since February 28, and Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for Gulf oil, largely shut. Talks through Qatar ended without a breakthrough on Monday, and President Trump has not ruled out new strikes.
beats.happened: On Thursday Iran sent the US a nuclear proposal via Qatar. Mohsen Rezaei, a top Iranian security official, said Iran will neither reopen Hormuz nor negotiate until its seven conditions, including lifting sanctions, freeing frozen assets and war reparations, are carried out. Washington wants nuclear issues in the first round.
beats.means: It keeps a diplomatic channel open, but the two sides still disagree on what comes first, so a deal is not close. Oil supply through Hormuz stays at risk either way.
beats.fx: A small push toward lower oil and calmer markets, weighed against Iran's hard conditions; oil-sensitive currencies such as the yen and Canadian dollar would feel any real progress first.

impact.why: Talks stay alive, but Iran won't reopen Hormuz until its demands are met.
Japan imports almost all its oil, so any real progress would ease a drag on the yen.
Oil is Canada's main export; the price outlook moves with these talks.

items.watch: Washington's reply to the proposal, and any sign that Trump picks renewed strikes over talks.

items.headline: Cleveland Fed's Hammack says US rates need to rise further, in small, steady steps
items.story_title: Fed: the case for a December rate rise
items.summary: Beth Hammack, head of the Cleveland Federal Reserve, said on Thursday that US rates should rise further to bring down inflation, preferably in quarter-point steps spread over several meetings.

beats.was: The Federal Reserve held its rate at 3.75%-4% last week, but Hammack was one of two officials who voted for a rise. The Fed's preferred inflation gauge was 3.6% in September, and 3.1% without food and energy, well above the 2% goal.
beats.happened: Speaking at a conference held by the Swiss National Bank's watchers in Zurich, Hammack said inflation is broad and rates must move high enough to slow the economy. She favours small, frequent rises so the Fed does not fall behind. Markets put the chance of a December quarter-point rise at about 69%.
beats.means: Hammack already voted for a rise, so her view is not new, but it shows the hawks at the Fed are not backing down after the midterms. It keeps a December rise as the most likely outcome.
beats.fx: Talk of further US rate rises gives the dollar some support at a time when the election result and a stock slump are pulling it lower.

impact.why: A known hawk repeats that rates should keep rising; mostly already priced.
Higher US rates make gold, which pays no interest, less attractive.

items.watch: Friday's US jobs report, which could firm up or weaken the case for a December rise.

items.headline: US stocks slump, Nasdaq down about 5%, as chipmakers sink and wipe out the post-election rally
items.story_title: The AI and chip stock selloff after the US midterms
items.summary: US stocks fell hard on Thursday, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq down about 5% and the S&P 500 down more than 3%, as chipmaker shares dropped and erased Wednesday's post-election gains.

beats.was: Democrats won both houses of the US Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections. Investors worry a Democratic Congress will bring tighter rules on artificial intelligence and data centers, the spending that has powered US stocks this year; chip shares in Seoul and Tokyo already fell early Thursday.
beats.happened: A US index of chipmaker shares fell about 11%, led by Nvidia, Micron, Broadcom and AMD, and Arm fell nearly 11% after weaker royalty income. Tesla and SpaceX dropped more than 9%. The VIX, a gauge of how much turbulence investors expect in US stocks, jumped more than 50%, and the 10-year US Treasury yield slipped to about 4.83%.
beats.means: Wednesday's relief rally was short-lived. A deep fall in the market's favourite shares hits confidence broadly and adds to worries that US growth slows if AI spending is cut back.
beats.fx: Sharp stock drops usually lift safe havens such as the Japanese yen and Swiss franc and weigh on currencies tied to global growth, like the Australian and New Zealand dollars. Lower US yields also take some support from the US dollar.

impact.why: Investors fleeing risky assets tend to buy the yen, and US yields fell.
The Australian dollar tends to fall when global stocks slump.
Fear in markets brings some demand for the franc as a safe haven.
Like the Aussie, the kiwi suffers when investors cut risk.
Lower US yields and worries about US growth weigh on the dollar.

items.watch: Whether the chip selloff spreads into Friday's US jobs report, and whether the yen strengthens further.

items.headline: Oil climbs back to about $97 a barrel after a two-month low, as a tanker hits a mine near Hormuz
items.story_title: Oil and the Iran war after the US midterms
items.summary: Brent crude rose about 2.5% to near $97 a barrel on Thursday, recovering part of this week's slide, after Iran's navy said a tanker east of the Strait of Hormuz struck a mine and caught fire.

beats.was: Oil fell to a two-month low on Wednesday, with Brent briefly near $93, on bets that Democratic control of the US Congress pushes Washington to end the US-Israel war with Iran. The war has disrupted tanker traffic through Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil.
beats.happened: Brent rose to about $97 and US crude to near $90, cutting the week's loss to about 14%. Ole Hansen, commodity strategist at Saxo Bank, said that without a peace deal oil can still swing sharply either way. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, spoke with his Saudi and Qatari counterparts.
beats.means: The quick bounce shows the market does not trust the peace bet yet. Supply of refined fuels such as diesel has also not recovered as fast as crude exports from the Gulf.
beats.fx: Firmer oil helps the Canadian dollar, Canada's main export, and raises import bills for Japan and the euro zone.

impact.why: A mined tanker and no peace deal pull prices back up from a two-month low.
Higher oil prices lift Canada's export earnings.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so dearer crude raises its import bill.

items.watch: Whether more ships are hit near Hormuz and whether Washington moves toward talks or new strikes.

items.headline: Three more tankers hit near Hormuz as sources say Trump may still restart strikes on Iran
items.story_title: Hormuz: shipping attacks and the oil supply
items.summary: Iran said three more tankers were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, and two people familiar with the matter told Reuters that President Trump is still likely to order new strikes on Iran.

beats.was: The US-Israel war with Iran has disrupted tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the channel for about a fifth of the world's oil. Oil fell more than $20 a barrel in a week on bets that Democratic control of the US Congress, won in Tuesday's midterms, pushes Washington to end the war.
beats.happened: Iran's Revolutionary Guards, who rarely own up to firing on merchant ships, said two tankers hit naval mines and a third caught fire. The UK navy's shipping office counts at least five ships hit since Sunday, close to October's pace, the worst month of the war. Two sources told Reuters Trump only held off on strikes until after the vote; there is no confirmed decision, and talks through Qatar have made no breakthrough.
beats.means: The peace bet that drove oil down sits next to rising attacks at sea and talk of renewed US bombing. The danger to Gulf supply has not gone away, so the recent drop in oil is fragile.
beats.fx: Oil steadied a little on Thursday. A confirmed US strike or more ship losses would lift oil, help the Canadian dollar and safe havens such as the Swiss franc, and weigh on big oil buyers like Japan and the euro zone.

impact.why: More ships hit and talk of new US strikes threaten Gulf supply again.
A war that may flare up again keeps some demand for a safe haven.
Japan buys almost all its oil abroad, so supply risks raise its import bill.

items.watch: Whether Trump orders new strikes, and whether ship attacks near Hormuz keep rising.

items.headline: US jobless claims come in below forecasts and worker productivity jumps 3.6%
items.story_title: Fed: the case for a December rate rise
items.summary: Fewer Americans filed new jobless claims than expected last week, and output per hour worked rose 3.6% in the third quarter while labour costs per unit of output fell.

beats.was: The US Federal Reserve is weighing a rate rise in December to fight inflation near 3.7%. The dollar had just fallen to a one-month low after Democrats won both houses of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections.
beats.happened: Thursday's figures showed 189,000 new claims for unemployment benefits, below the roughly 197,000 forecast. Separately, productivity, the amount produced per hour of work, grew at a 3.6% yearly pace in July to September, well above forecasts near 2.8%, and unit labour costs fell 0.7% when a small rise was expected.
beats.means: Layoffs stay low, so the job market looks solid. Faster productivity and falling labour costs mean wages are adding less to inflation, which cuts both ways for the Fed: a firm economy backs a rise, softer cost pressure argues for patience.
beats.fx: The dollar firmed a little off its overnight low after the release, but the mixed message left it near one-month lows ahead of Friday's jobs report.

impact.why: Low jobless claims support the dollar, while falling labour costs ease the inflation case for a December Fed rise.

items.watch: Friday's official US jobs report for October, expected to show around 60,000 new jobs.

items.headline: Eurasia Group cuts its odds of a US-Iran deal to 10%, as oil steadies after an 8% drop
items.story_title: Hormuz: shipping attacks and the oil supply
items.summary: Political risk firm Eurasia Group now puts the chance of a US-Iran deal at just 10%, half its earlier view, and sees new US strikes as the most likely outcome. Brent recovered to about $96 a barrel.

beats.was: The US-Israel war with Iran has choked tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil. On Wednesday oil fell more than 8%, to its lowest since late August, on bets that the Democratic win in Tuesday's US midterm elections pushes Washington toward peace.
beats.happened: Eurasia Group, a firm that advises investors on political risk, lowered its odds of a deal to 10% from 20%, put renewed US strikes at 60% and a drawn-out standoff at 30%. It says Iran has not budged on its demands and President Trump is unlikely to accept terms that look like a defeat. Citi also warned the White House could act on its own before the new Congress sits in January.
beats.means: Wednesday's slide priced a path to peace that this firm now sees as unlikely. If its view is right, the risk to Gulf supply lasts longer than the oil price suggests; it estimates Brent at $110 to $125 if fighting escalates.
beats.fx: This is an outside forecast, not news of a decision, so its pull is mild. It leans toward higher oil, which helps the Canadian dollar and safe havens such as the Swiss franc and hurts big oil buyers like Japan.

impact.why: A respected forecaster sees peace as unlikely and new US strikes as more likely.
Lower odds of a deal keep some demand for a safe haven.
Japan imports nearly all its oil, so a longer war raises its fuel bill.

items.watch: Whether Trump orders new strikes on Iran before the new Congress takes its seats in January.

items.headline: Bank of England raises rates to 4%, its first hike since 2023, as energy bites
items.story_title: Bank of England's first rate rise since 2023
items.summary: The Bank of England raised its rate to 4% from 3.75%, its first rise since 2023, and now sees UK inflation peaking near 5% next year as the Iran war lifts energy costs.

beats.was: The Bank of England had not raised rates since August 2023 and held at 3.75% in September, when three of its nine policymakers already wanted a rise. UK inflation then climbed to 3.5% as fuel and gas costs jumped with the Iran war.
beats.happened: On Thursday the Bank lifted its rate by a quarter point to 4%, with almost all policymakers in favour. Its staff now expect inflation to reach about 5% by the middle of next year, far above its earlier forecasts. Governor Andrew Bailey said that without real progress toward ending the Middle East conflict he could see the case for another rise, but the Bank did not commit to a set path.
beats.means: The rise itself was expected. The new news is a much higher inflation forecast and an open door to more rises tied to the war, which leans toward the market's view of further increases rather than one and done.
beats.fx: A higher inflation forecast and talk of possible further rises support the pound; a real step toward peace in the Middle East would weaken that case.

impact.why: A sharply higher inflation forecast and a door left open to more rises back the pound.
Another central bank raising rates on energy costs keeps a European Central Bank rise in view, but the pound gains more against the euro.

items.watch: The next decision on 17 December, UK inflation figures, and any progress toward ending the Iran war, which Bailey tied to the rate outlook.

items.headline: Brent recovers to about $96 after its steepest one-day fall in months
items.story_title: Oil and the Iran war after the US midterms
items.summary: Brent crude rose about 1.5% to near $96 a barrel on Thursday, a small bounce after Wednesday's drop of more than 8% on hopes the Iran war heads toward talks.

beats.was: Brent was near $118 a barrel on 30 October because the US-Israeli war with Iran has choked oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. On Wednesday it fell more than 8% to its lowest in over two months after Democrats won the US Congress, raising bets on a diplomatic end.
beats.happened: On Thursday Brent rose about $1.40 to roughly $96 and US crude edged up to about $88.50. President Trump said there are no immediate plans for new strikes but did not rule them out.
beats.means: The bounce is small next to Wednesday's fall, so traders still lean toward a settlement, but with no deal signed some buyers are stepping back in.
beats.fx: A steadier oil price gives a little support to oil-linked currencies such as the Canadian dollar; the bigger driver is still whether talks with Iran actually start.

impact.why: A modest rebound after a heavy sell-off, with no peace deal yet.
Firmer oil eases pressure on Canada's main export.

items.watch: Any formal start of US-Iran talks, new attacks on ships near Hormuz, and weekly US crude stock figures.

items.headline: German factory orders bounce 4.4% in September, a little short of forecasts
items.story_title: Germany's factory orders swing back
items.summary: New orders at German factories rose 4.4% in September after a 10.6% drop in August, a solid rebound but slightly below the 4.8% economists expected.

beats.was: German factory orders swing hard from month to month because a few very large public contracts, such as defence and infrastructure, land at once. In August they fell 10.6% after earlier big gains.
beats.happened: Germany's statistics office said on Thursday that orders rose 4.4% in September from August, after adjusting for seasons and working days. Economists polled by Reuters had expected 4.8%.
beats.means: The rebound undoes less than half of August's fall, so it reads as normal lumpiness rather than a new upturn in Europe's biggest economy.
beats.fx: A small miss on a noisy figure barely changes the outlook for the euro, which is moving far more on the dollar and on inflation.

impact.why: A rebound in orders, but smaller than expected and not enough to undo August's slump.

items.watch: German industrial output on Friday and whether large public orders keep coming in coming months.

items.headline: Gold rises to about $4,135, its highest since late October, ahead of the US jobs report
items.story_title: Gold after the US midterms
items.summary: Gold kept climbing in Asian trade on Thursday to about $4,135 an ounce, its highest since 22 October, with the dollar holding near a one-month low.

beats.was: Gold jumped about 3.5% on Wednesday after Democrats won both houses of the US Congress, which pushed the dollar and US bond yields down. Gold usually gains when the dollar and yields fall.
beats.happened: Early on Thursday spot gold reached about $4,135, adding roughly another 2%. Markets still see about an 80% chance the Federal Reserve raises rates in December.
beats.means: The rebound is carrying on rather than fading, but it rests on a weaker dollar, and the US jobs report on Friday will test that.
beats.fx: Gold has upward pressure while the dollar stays soft; a strong jobs report that firms up a December Fed rise would work against it.

impact.why: Follow-through buying after Wednesday's jump, helped by a dollar near a one-month low.
Gold's climb mirrors the dollar staying weak after the midterms.

items.watch: Friday's US jobs report (forecast around 65,000) and any change in odds of a December Fed rise.

items.headline: Yen edges below 158 per dollar as chip stocks slide in Seoul and Tokyo
items.story_title: US midterms: a week of elections, central banks and jobs data risk
items.summary: The dollar slipped under 158 yen early Thursday as chipmakers sold off across Asia on fears a Democratic Congress will rein in the AI boom.

beats.was: Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections. Investors fear tighter rules on artificial intelligence, which has driven big gains in Asian chip stocks this year.
beats.happened: South Korea's Kospi fell about 3.5% by late morning, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix down 6-7%, and Japan's Nikkei slipped 0.5% as chip-test and equipment makers fell sharply. Hong Kong and Australian shares rose. The dollar eased to about 157.96 yen from 158.41, and Brent crude dipped below $94.
beats.means: Money is moving out of the AI trade that did best under Republican rule, while the wider market still takes the election calmly.
beats.fx: Selling of risky assets plus lower US yields gives the yen mild support, though the move is small.

impact.why: A small move as chip stocks fall and the dollar softens.
Brent drifts a little lower after Wednesday's big drop.

items.watch: Whether the chip sell-off spreads beyond Korea and Japan when Europe opens.

items.headline: Australia's trade surplus jumps to A$2.8 billion, a seven-month high
items.story_title: Reserve Bank of Australia: a fifth rate rise this year?
items.summary: Australia sold far more abroad than it bought in September, as gas and metals exports rose and gold imports dropped sharply.

beats.was: Australia's goods trade surplus had shrunk to under A$0.2 billion in August, and forecasts for September were about A$1 billion. The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its rate to 4.85% on Tuesday.
beats.happened: The September surplus widened to about A$2.8 billion, the biggest in seven months. Exports rose 2.3%, led by liquefied natural gas and metals, while imports fell 3.3%, mostly because gold imports dropped by about a third.
beats.means: Stronger exports help Australia's growth, but gold shipments swing a lot from month to month, so the jump overstates the real improvement. On its own it is unlikely to change the rate outlook.
beats.fx: More foreign income gives the Australian dollar mild support, but slowing China and a central bank that has signalled a pause matter more.

impact.why: A big trade beat, but flattered by volatile gold flows.

items.watch: Whether gas and metals exports stay strong once gold flows settle.

items.headline: Bank of England expected to raise rates to 4% on Thursday, its first rise in three years
items.story_title: Bank of England's first rate rise since 2023
items.summary: Economists polled by Reuters expect the Bank of England to lift its rate to 4% from 3.75% today, with seven of nine policymakers voting for it.

beats.was: The Bank of England has not raised rates since August 2023. In September it held at 3.75%, but three of its nine policymakers already wanted a rise, and UK inflation then climbed to 3.5%, well above the Bank's own forecast, as the Iran war pushed up fuel and gas costs.
beats.happened: Ahead of Thursday's decision at noon London time, economists expect a 7-2 vote for a rise to 4%. Markets go further and price at least three more quarter-point rises next year, while many economists, including PIMCO's, expect only one more early next year and then a long pause.
beats.means: The rise itself is almost fully expected. What matters is whether the Bank's new forecasts and wording back the market's path of several more rises or lean toward the economists' view of one more and done.
beats.fx: A rise with hints of more would support the pound; a split vote or talk of a pause could pull it back from its highest level since mid-September.

impact.why: The rise is expected; the guidance on what comes next decides the pound's move.

items.watch: The vote split and whether the Bank's new forecasts show inflation peaking above 4% next year.

items.headline: Canadian dollar reaches a seven-week high on a bigger trade surplus and a weaker US dollar
items.story_title: Canada: trade, oil and the loonie
items.summary: The Canadian dollar rose about 0.3% to near C$1.3965 per US dollar, its strongest since mid-September, after Canada's September trade surplus came in well above forecasts and the US dollar slid on the midterm results.

beats.was: Canada sends most of its exports to the US, so its trade balance is a quick check on how US tariffs and oil prices are hitting the economy. The US dollar has been falling since Democrats won both houses of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections.
beats.happened: Statistics Canada said the goods trade surplus widened to about C$5.35 billion in September, against roughly C$4.1 billion expected, and August was revised up. Export volumes still fell 4%, and a separate survey showed Canada's services sector shrank for a fifth month in October. The loonie touched C$1.3930 during the day.
beats.means: The bigger surplus came partly from imports falling, not exports booming, so it is a modest sign of strength rather than a turnaround. The loonie's gain is notable because oil, Canada's main export, fell about 8% on the same day.
beats.fx: Supports the Canadian dollar for now, with most of the push coming from a weaker US dollar. Cheaper oil is the main force pulling the other way.

impact.why: A clear trade beat and a falling US dollar lifted it to a seven-week high.
The US dollar's broad slide after the midterms did much of the work.
The loonie rose even as oil fell, showing the link is loose today.

items.watch: Canada's October jobs report on Friday, November 6, and whether oil keeps falling as Iran peace talks go on.

items.headline: Dollar falls to a one-month low as Democratic wins raise worries about tighter AI rules
items.story_title: US midterms: a week of elections, central banks and jobs data
items.summary: The dollar index slipped to about 101.4, a one-month low, as investors worried a Democratic Congress could tighten rules on artificial intelligence, the spending that has driven much of US growth.

beats.was: US growth this year has leaned heavily on company spending on AI and data centres. Strong US data had markets expecting a December Federal Reserve rate rise, which supported the dollar.
beats.happened: After Democrats won the House and the Senate on Tuesday, the dollar index fell to 101.41. The euro rose 0.4% to $1.1236, the pound rose 0.46% to $1.3475, a seven-week high, and the dollar slipped to 158.09 yen and 0.8162 Swiss francs. The 10-year Treasury yield eased to about 4.92%.
beats.means: Investors fear tougher AI rules could slow growth and lessen the need for Fed rate rises. Strategists at Convera and OCBC bank noted that passing laws stays hard while President Trump holds a veto, so yields and economic data matter more than politics for the dollar.
beats.fx: Mild pressure on the dollar against every major currency; a Commonwealth Bank of Australia strategist said a sharp rise in oil is the main thing that would lift it again.

impact.why: Worries that tighter AI rules slow US growth and the need for rate rises.
Pound at a seven-week high as the dollar slips.
Euro at its highest in nearly two weeks.

items.watch: Friday's US jobs report for October, and whether AI-linked US stocks keep falling.

items.headline: Gold ends the day about 3% higher near $4,060 as the dollar falls
items.story_title: Gold: Fed rate-rise bets vs a weaker dollar
items.summary: Gold finished Wednesday up about 3.3% near $4,063 an ounce, one of its best days in months, as the dollar and US bond yields fell after Democrats won control of Congress.

beats.was: Gold fell through October to near its lowest in a year as markets came to expect a December rate rise from the US Federal Reserve, since higher rates make gold, which pays no interest, less attractive.
beats.happened: After Democrats won both the House and the Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections, the dollar index fell to about 101.5 and the 10-year US Treasury yield slipped to about 4.89%. Gold built on its early gains through the US session; silver also rose sharply.
beats.means: Markets expect a split government to borrow less, which keeps yields lower and the dollar softer, both good for gold. A December Fed rate rise is still seen as likely, so the rebound rests on the dollar staying weak.
beats.fx: Gold's jump is the mirror image of the dollar's slide to a one-month low.

impact.why: A 3% one-day jump as the dollar and yields fall.
Part of the same broad dollar slide after the midterms.

items.watch: Friday's US jobs report for October, which will shape December Fed rate-rise bets.

items.headline: Iran readies a response plan for any new US attack as another tanker is hit near Hormuz
items.story_title: Hormuz: shipping attacks and the oil supply
items.summary: Iran said it has a plan ready to hit back at once against any new US attack, while a tanker was struck by two unidentified projectiles near the Strait of Hormuz, the British navy's shipping office said.

beats.was: The US-Israel war with Iran has disrupted tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the channel for about a fifth of the world's oil. Peace talks through Qatar and Pakistan are under way, and markets now expect the new Democratic Congress to push for an end to the war.
beats.happened: Iran's military said it is updating its list of targets to include US and Israeli sites across a wider area. UK Maritime Trade Operations, which tracks Gulf shipping, reported a tanker hit by two projectiles near the strait; Iran's Revolutionary Guards separately said three tankers had exploded on mines after crossing without permission. These claims have not been independently confirmed.
beats.means: The waters around Hormuz remain dangerous even as diplomacy moves ahead, which keeps shipping and insurance costs high. Oil still fell about 9% on the day, so for now traders are betting on peace more than on new supply losses.
beats.fx: Any confirmed hit to Gulf supply would lift oil and help the Canadian dollar, while weighing on big oil buyers like Japan and the euro zone.

impact.why: Fresh attacks on shipping, but oil fell anyway on peace bets.
Continued fighting keeps some demand for safe havens.

items.watch: Whether ships keep crossing Hormuz safely and whether the US-Iran talks set a next meeting.

items.headline: Bank of Japan minutes show the board backed more rate rises, one member floated a faster pace
items.story_title: Japan: guarding the yen near 160 per dollar
items.summary: The record of the Bank of Japan's September meeting shows members agreed to keep raising rates, and one said the pace may need to quicken if prices run too hot.

beats.was: In September the Bank of Japan raised its rate to 1.25%, the highest since 1995, by a 7-2 vote; two members wanted to wait. It held in October, and markets have been weighing another rise in December.
beats.happened: Minutes released Thursday morning in Tokyo show members agreed to keep lifting rates as underlying inflation nears the 2% goal. One member said rises may need to speed up if prices overshoot; others noted oil up about 50% since July. The government's Cabinet Office asked the bank to weigh the build-up of past rises carefully.
beats.means: The board sounds set on more rises, and the talk of a faster pace is new. It supports the view that December is a live meeting, though the government's call for care is a brake.
beats.fx: A keener Bank of Japan helps the yen, which sits near 158 per dollar, close to the 160 area where Tokyo has stepped in before.

impact.why: Minutes lean toward more rate rises, but they look back to September and add little to December pricing.

items.watch: Whether Bank of Japan officials repeat the faster-pace idea in speeches before the December meeting.

items.headline: Oil plunges about 8%, Brent near $95, as markets bet the Iran war winds down
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Brent crude fell about 8.5% to near $95 a barrel and US crude dropped below $89, the lowest in almost two months, as traders bet that Democratic control of Congress pushes Washington toward ending the war with Iran.

beats.was: The US-Israel war with Iran has kept oil above $100 for weeks by choking tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the main exit for Gulf oil. Democrats won both houses of the US Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections, and many voters blamed the war for high fuel prices.
beats.happened: Brent fell 8.5% to $94.83 and US crude (WTI) fell 7.5% to $88.88 in Wednesday's US session, more than 15% lower over the week. Peace talks through Qatar and Pakistan have resumed, though Iran's leadership said anyone expecting a US policy shift after the vote is mistaken.
beats.means: A large part of the war premium is coming out of the price on the view that the new Congress will limit funding for the war. Gulf exports had already been recovering, so supply looks less tight. Any new strike or attack on shipping could reverse much of the drop quickly.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil hurts the Canadian dollar, since oil is Canada's main export, and helps big oil buyers like Japan and the euro zone. It also eases the inflation worry behind the Federal Reserve's expected December rate rise.

impact.why: The biggest one-day fall in months as bets grow that the war ends.
Much lower prices for Canada's main export.
Japan buys almost all its oil abroad, so a smaller import bill helps the yen.

items.watch: Any new US strike or attack on Gulf shipping, and whether the US-Iran talks set a next meeting.

items.headline: Vice President Vance says the Iran war cost Republicans the midterms
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: US Vice President JD Vance said voter anger over the Iran war was the main reason Republicans lost both houses of Congress, and backed calls for a diplomatic end to the fighting.

beats.was: The US has been at war with Iran for months, and fuel prices have soared. Democrats won control of the Senate and the House in Tuesday's midterm elections.
beats.happened: In his first comments since the results, Vance wrote on X that the war was the reason his party lost, and called a diplomatic resolution sensible. He led US negotiators in spring talks whose deal later collapsed. President Trump said the war will end when he decides it ends.
beats.means: A senior figure in the administration openly blaming the war adds to the sense that Washington wants a way out, which helped drive Wednesday's oil slide. It is a signal, not a policy change: Trump still controls the decision.
beats.fx: Talk of ending the war lowers oil prices and cuts demand for safe havens like the Swiss franc and gold.

impact.why: A top official backing diplomacy raises the odds the war ends.
Less need for a safe place to park money if the war winds down.

items.watch: Whether the White House changes its Iran stance, and the next round of talks through Qatar and Pakistan.

items.headline: US crude stocks fall only slightly, far less than an industry survey suggested
items.story_title: Hormuz: shipping attacks and the oil supply
items.summary: Official US government figures showed crude oil stocks fell by about 0.9 million barrels last week, a much smaller drop than the 5.3 million barrel fall an industry survey reported on Tuesday.

beats.was: The US-Israel war with Iran has disrupted tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, keeping oil above $100 a barrel. Weekly US stock figures show how tight supply is; Tuesday's industry survey from the American Petroleum Institute hinted at a big drawdown.
beats.happened: The Energy Information Administration, the US government's energy statistics agency, said commercial crude stocks fell about 0.9 million barrels in the week to October 30.
beats.means: US supply looks less tight than Tuesday's survey implied, which takes a little support away from prices. Talks between Washington and Tehran still matter far more than one week of stock data.
beats.fx: A small weight on oil is a small weight on the Canadian dollar, since oil is Canada's main export.

impact.why: A smaller fall in stocks than the industry survey pointed to.
Slightly less support for Canada's main export.

items.watch: Any news on US-Iran talks or new attacks on shipping near the Strait of Hormuz.

items.headline: US services growth eases a little in October, slightly below forecasts
items.story_title: Fed: the case for a December rate rise
items.summary: The Institute for Supply Management's survey of US service firms slipped to 54.5 in October from 54.9, just under the 54.8 expected, but hiring improved and every part of the survey still showed growth.

beats.was: Services are most of the US economy. Strong figures this week, including a jump in job openings, have kept markets expecting the Federal Reserve to raise rates in December to fight inflation.
beats.happened: The survey read 54.5 (above 50 means growth). New orders and business activity slowed, while the hiring gauge rose to 51.4 and the prices firms pay stayed very high at 73. The survey said many firms have not yet passed tariff and fuel costs on to customers.
beats.means: Services are still growing at a healthy pace and price pressure is not fading, so this does little to weaken the case for a December Fed rate rise. The dollar barely moved.
beats.fx: A neutral print for the dollar: it neither adds to nor reverses today's slide after the midterm results.

impact.why: Slightly softer growth, but firmer hiring and high prices keep a December Fed rise on the table.

items.watch: The US jobs report on Friday, November 6, the last big test before the Fed's December decision.

items.headline: US private employers add 86,000 jobs in October, a little more than expected
items.story_title: Fed: the case for a December rate rise
items.summary: The ADP survey of US private payrolls showed 86,000 new jobs in October, slightly above forecasts and the same pace as September, with pay for people who switch jobs still rising fast.

beats.was: The US Federal Reserve is weighing a rate rise in December to fight inflation running near 3.7%. Monthly hiring has been slow, so each jobs survey is read for whether the economy can take a higher rate.
beats.happened: ADP, a payroll company, said private employers added 86,000 jobs in October against forecasts of roughly 70,000 to 75,000. Shops, transport and health care hired; business services cut jobs. Pay for job switchers rose 4.8% from a year earlier.
beats.means: Hiring is modest but steady, and pay is still growing quickly, which supports the case for a December rate rise. It is only a preview: the government's official jobs report on Friday, November 6, matters more.
beats.fx: A slightly firmer jobs picture gives the dollar some support, but it was drowned out by the slide after Tuesday's midterm results.

impact.why: A small hiring beat that keeps a December Fed rate rise likely.

items.watch: Friday's official US jobs report for October, expected to show around 60,000 new jobs.

items.headline: US Treasury keeps its quarterly bond sales unchanged at $125 billion
items.story_title: US midterms: a week of elections, central banks and jobs data
items.summary: The US Treasury said it will sell $125 billion of longer-dated debt next week, the same amount and mix as last quarter, so there is no new supply of bonds to push US yields higher.

beats.was: Every three months the US Treasury, which manages the government's borrowing, says how much longer-term debt it will sell. Bigger sales can lift US interest rates, and the dollar with them. Yields had already fallen this week after Democrats won Congress, on bets a split government borrows less.
beats.happened: On Wednesday morning the Treasury kept its quarterly sale of notes and bonds at $125 billion and left the mix of maturities unchanged, in line with what dealers expected.
beats.means: No surprise, so it adds nothing new to the fall in US yields. It confirms the government is not leaning harder on long-term borrowing for now.
beats.fx: Neutral for the dollar. It removes one possible source of upward pressure on US yields but does not add a new push either way.

impact.why: As expected; no extra bond supply to lift yields, and no new reason for them to fall.

items.watch: Demand at next week's US bond sales, and the US jobs report on Friday, November 6.

items.headline: Oil turns lower, Brent near $101, as a Democratic Congress may limit US action on Iran
items.story_title: Iran: talks in Tehran vs the threat of new US strikes
items.summary: Brent crude gave up an early gain and fell about 2% to near $101.65 a barrel, as traders weighed whether a Democratic Congress will hold back new US military action against Iran.

beats.was: The US-Israel war with Iran has pushed oil above $100 a barrel by disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for Gulf oil. Prices fell 7% on Monday when Iran signalled it was open to peace talks.
beats.happened: Brent fell 1.9% to $101.65 and US crude (WTI) fell 1.9% to $94.33 in a swinging session. Analysts said Democratic control of both houses of Congress could restrict President Trump's foreign policy, including money for military operations abroad. Qatar said its mediation between Washington and Tehran goes on, with no breakthrough yet.
beats.means: Some of the war-risk premium is leaving the price as new US strikes look less likely. But Neil Shearing, chief economist at Capital Economics, warned that renewed strikes could lift Brent above $120, so prices can still swing hard.
beats.fx: Cheaper oil weighs on the Canadian dollar, since oil is Canada's main export, and eases price pressure for big oil buyers like Japan and the euro zone.

impact.why: Less chance of new US strikes takes some war premium out of the price.
Lower prices for Canada's main export.

items.watch: Official US oil stock figures at 9:30 a.m. CT today, and any sign of new US strikes or a deal with Iran.

items.headline: Euro-zone inflation rises to 4.0% in October, as expected
items.story_title: ECB: a December rate rise to fight energy-driven inflation
items.summary: Prices in the 20 countries that use the euro rose 4.0% over the past year in October, up from 3.8%, matching forecasts. Energy did most of the lifting.

beats.was: Energy costs have climbed since the Iran war disrupted Gulf oil and gas, pushing euro-zone inflation to about double the European Central Bank's 2% goal. The ECB has signalled it could raise rates in December.
beats.happened: Eurostat, the EU's statistics office, said in its first estimate that inflation rose to 4.0% in October, as economists expected. Inflation without energy, food, alcohol and tobacco held at 2.5%, also as expected, while energy prices were about 21% higher than a year ago.
beats.means: The rise comes from energy, not from broader price pressure, since the underlying measure did not move. That keeps a December ECB rate rise possible but adds no new urgency.
beats.fx: No surprise, so little fresh push for the euro either way; the euro's gains today come from the weaker dollar.

impact.why: In line with forecasts: higher inflation backs a possible rate rise, but steady underlying prices add no urgency.

items.watch: The ECB decision on December 17, and whether energy prices keep rising.

items.headline: Gold climbs back above $4,000 as the dollar and US yields fall after the midterms
items.story_title: Gold: Fed rate-rise bets vs a weaker dollar
items.summary: Gold rose about 2% and crossed back above $4,000 an ounce as the dollar fell to a one-month low after Democrats won both houses of the US Congress.

beats.was: Gold slid in October to about $3,870 last Friday, near its lowest in a year, as markets came to expect a December rate rise from the US Federal Reserve. Higher rates make gold, which pays no interest, less attractive.
beats.happened: December gold futures traded near $4,027 early Wednesday, up 2.2% from Tuesday, and spot gold crossed $4,000, after Democrats won the House and the Senate. The dollar index fell to about 101.5, Treasury yields dropped, and silver jumped about 4%.
beats.means: A split government is expected to borrow less, which keeps US yields lower and helps gold. Markets still put the chance of a December Fed rate rise near 78%, so the bounce depends on the dollar staying weak.
beats.fx: A weaker dollar and lower yields lift gold; this is a rebound, and the Fed headwind has not gone away.

impact.why: Back above $4,000 as the dollar and US yields fall.
Gold's jump mirrors the dollar's slide to a one-month low.

items.watch: Friday's US jobs report for October, which will shape December Fed rate-rise bets.

items.headline: Democrats take control of the US Senate after winning key midterm races
items.story_title: US midterms: a week of elections, central banks and jobs data
items.summary: Democrats won back the US Senate on Tuesday night, taking Republican seats from Iowa to Texas. With the House also going their way, President Trump faces a Congress run by the other party.

beats.was: Before Tuesday's midterm elections, President Trump's Republicans held both the Senate and the House, which let them pass tax cuts and spending with little resistance. Democrats needed to gain four Senate seats, which looked hard.
beats.happened: The Associated Press reported that Democrats retook the Senate, winning Republican-held or open seats in North Carolina, Ohio, Texas, Kansas, South Carolina and Iowa. US networks had already projected a Democratic House, and the AP called the House for Democrats early Wednesday.
beats.means: A Democratic Congress can block new tax cuts and big spending plans for the rest of Mr Trump's term, so the US is likely to borrow less than it would have. Less borrowing points to lower US bond yields over time.
beats.fx: Lower expected yields take some support from the dollar, which slipped to a one-month low in Asian trading as the results came in.

impact.why: A Congress controlled by Democrats means less new borrowing and lower yields, which weighs on the dollar.
Lower US yields make gold, which pays no interest, a little more appealing.
The euro rose to about $1.125 as the dollar fell on the results.

items.watch: Whether US bond yields keep falling, and whether Friday's US jobs report keeps a December Federal Reserve rate rise likely.

items.headline: Democrats projected to win control of the US House of Representatives
items.story_title: US midterms: a week of elections, central banks and jobs data
items.summary: US networks projected late Tuesday that Democrats will take the House from President Trump's Republicans; the Senate is still too close to call.

beats.was: Americans voted on Tuesday in the midterm elections, which decide all 435 House seats and 35 of 100 Senate seats. Republicans held both chambers, which let President Trump pass tax cuts and spending with little resistance.
beats.happened: Major US networks projected just before 10 p.m. Eastern that Democrats will win a House majority. In the Senate, Democrat Roy Cooper took a Republican seat in North Carolina, but control was still open, and a 50-50 split would leave Republicans in charge through Vice President JD Vance's tie-breaking vote.
beats.means: A Democratic House can block new tax cuts and big spending plans from next year, which points to less government borrowing and lower US bond yields. Much of this was expected, so the Senate result now decides how big the shift is.
beats.fx: Lower expected yields weigh on the dollar; a Democratic Senate as well would add to that pressure.

impact.why: A split government means less borrowing and lower yields, which takes some support from the dollar.
Lower US yields make gold, which pays no interest, a little more attractive.

items.watch: Whether Democrats also win the Senate, and whether the Associated Press confirms the House call.

items.headline: Japan's Nikkei drops 3% as Democratic gains in the US midterms hit AI stocks
items.story_title: US midterms: a week of elections, central banks and jobs data
items.summary: Tokyo's main share index fell about 3% on Wednesday, led by chip and AI names, on worry that a Democratic Congress will tighten rules on data centres.

beats.was: Japanese shares had climbed to records this year on the boom in artificial-intelligence spending, with chip and cable makers among the biggest winners.
beats.happened: The Nikkei 225 fell 3.1% to about 61,128 early Wednesday. SoftBank Group lost about 7%, memory maker Kioxia 10% and chip-testing firm Advantest 6.4%, as investors bet Democrats would bring tighter rules on data-centre projects.
beats.means: A sharp fall in stocks tends to send money toward safe assets, and the yen usually benefits when Japanese investors pull back from risk.
beats.fx: Mild support for the yen through risk aversion, against the much bigger pull of the gap between US and Japanese interest rates.

impact.why: Falling stocks tend to send money into the yen as a safe place.
The Australian dollar tends to slip when Asian stocks sell off.

items.watch: Whether the sell-off spreads to US stocks when New York opens on Wednesday.

items.headline: Stocks and the dollar slide after early Democratic wins in the US midterms
items.story_title: US midterms: a week of elections, central banks and jobs data
items.summary: The dollar fell about 0.3% and US bond yields dropped as early midterm results favoured the Democrats, lifting the euro and pound.

beats.was: The dollar had firmed earlier on Tuesday after strong US job-openings and factory figures, which raised the odds of a Federal Reserve rate rise in December.
beats.happened: As Democrats won key Senate races in Georgia and North Carolina, the dollar index, which tracks the dollar against six major currencies, fell 0.3% to about 101.4. The 10-year US Treasury yield dropped about 6 basis points to 4.91%, the euro rose 0.4% to about $1.124 and the pound 0.4% to about $1.346.
beats.means: Traders read Democratic gains as a check on government borrowing, which lowers the yields that have been pulling money into the dollar.
beats.fx: The euro and pound gain most directly from a softer dollar; how far it goes depends on the Senate count.

impact.why: Falling Treasury yields on Democratic gains pulled the dollar lower across the board.
The euro rose to about $1.124 as the dollar weakened.
The pound rose to about $1.346 ahead of Thursday's expected Bank of England rate rise.

items.watch: Friday's US jobs report, which could restore the dollar's support if it is strong.

items.headline: China's services growth slows to a three-month low in October
items.story_title: China: a slowing economy
items.summary: China's private services survey fell to 50.8 in October from 51.6, still growing but at the slowest pace in three months.

beats.was: China's private factory survey beat forecasts on Monday, but the wider economy has been uneven, with firms cutting prices to win customers.
beats.happened: The RatingDog China services PMI, a business survey where 50 separates growth from shrinking, fell to 50.8 from 51.6. Companies kept cutting prices while their costs, including oil and wages, rose at the fastest pace in five months, and their confidence dropped to a three-month low. The combined factory and services reading eased to 52.0 from 52.4.
beats.means: China's economy is still growing, but firms are squeezed between rising costs and price wars, which caps how much they buy from abroad.
beats.fx: A small drag on the Australian and New Zealand dollars, whose exports depend on Chinese demand.

impact.why: Slower Chinese services growth hints at softer demand for Australian exports.
China is New Zealand's biggest buyer, so slower growth there weighs on the kiwi.

items.watch: China's October trade figures, due later this week.

items.headline: Swiss inflation jumps to 1.5% in October on fuel costs
items.story_title: Switzerland: inflation picks up on fuel costs
items.summary: Swiss prices rose 1.5% from a year earlier in October, up from 1.0% and above the 1.3% expected, almost entirely because fuel got dearer; underlying prices stayed calm.

beats.was: Swiss inflation has been very low for two years, inside the Swiss National Bank's 0-2% target, and some traders had hoped the bank would cut its rate again in December. The Iran war has pushed fuel prices sharply higher this year.
beats.happened: The Federal Statistical Office said prices rose 0.2% in the month, against no change expected, and 1.5% over the year, the highest since late 2023. Petrol, diesel and heating oil drove nearly all of it. Core inflation, which leaves out energy and fresh food, held at just 0.5%.
beats.means: Higher headline inflation makes a December rate cut by the Swiss National Bank harder to argue for. But because the rise is in fuel and not in everyday prices, the bank is unlikely to feel pushed to raise rates.
beats.fx: Supports the Swiss franc by cutting the odds of a December rate cut; the calm core reading limits how far that goes.

impact.why: A clear beat that makes a December rate cut less likely.

items.watch: The Swiss National Bank's December 10 decision, and whether fuel costs keep rising.
